Fortunately, space-power theory has richly explored the nature of violence in space-power.

The most important space-power theorist to explore the nature of space warfare is John Klein. His 2006 book Space Warfare: Strategy, Principles, and Policy followed much of previous spacepower theory in accepting that space-power shares many common attributes to seapower, and Klein adapted British maritime theorist Julian Corbett to the space domain. But the concepts were not completely alike. With the advent of modern communications through the electromagnetic spectrum, Klein adjusted Corbett’s concept slightly and explained that there were both “physical” and “non-physical” CLOCs. Physical CLOCs were spacecraft and orbital trajectories and had direct analogies to the maritime domain. They were also tactile and easily understood. However, non-physical CLOCs were something fundamentally different than anything seen in classic seapower. “A key difference [between space and maritime LOCs] is that many of the things being communicated in space are not directly tangible in a conventional manner,” Klein argued.18 This key difference is from

Physical destructive weapons such as direct-ascent anti-satellite weapons are intended to destroy the space vehicle and eliminating access to the CLOC (indeed eliminating the CLOC itself) the satellite provides, an action against physical access and hence an attack on the physical CLOC.

Klein’s insights also connect space to space warfare with limited war. Klein argued, “limited aims include only those attempting to acquire certain lines of communications in space or assuring one’s access within a region of space, but they do not include the overthrow of a sovereign government.”21 Since space warfare proper is the attack and defense of CLOCs, space warfare in isolation can only be fought to achieve limited aims. Terrestrial strike from space is a use of space-power, not an act of space warfare, and can be used (in conjunction with other means) as a method of unlimited war, but not space warfare itself.

Klein blames the common but erroneous assumption that space is an offense-dominant domain on space technology and the lack of defensive concern that designers have for space systems, not the domain itself. Defense is indeed the stronger form of space war, “but to successfully assume a defensive posture, an advantageous position must be held.” Klein argues, “Placing space-based defensive systems in an unprotected, highly vulnerable location – as in a near-earth orbit – without any kind of relative advantage is not the strategy of the defense but is the strategy of the ludicrous.”27 Space systems have simply been built too weak and defenseless due to an overemphasis on cost over defensibility. Klein dismisses the offense-dominant argument by asserting that even though “spacebased systems seem highly vulnerable to offensive weapons, this is a transitory state of affairs within the latest technology cycle.”28 Sooner or later, defensive technology will be developed to overcome the offensive advantages of space weapons. The race between technologies of offense and defense has always been, and ever shall be.

Another critical defensive strength of the space domain not mentioned by Klein but absolutely relevant is the sheer altitude of spacecraft with respect to Earth weapons, including the “high ground” and “gravity well” effects. From extremely high altitudes, space systems can “see” earth objects in wider swaths than earth systems can see space objects. Furthermore, the orbiting space object will likely be able to see physical weapons launched from Earth (such as missiles) extremely easy if sufficiently equipped. These height advantages are significant so long as space systems are designed to take advantage of them. Likewise, objects orbiting in space, through the potential energy granted by extreme altitudes, are much more energetic than objects that must “rise out” of the Earth’s gravity well to reach the target. The gravity well may not significantly impact directed energy weapons (though other defensive methods are available), the energy requirements of an ascending weapon will accrue movement and maneuver advantages to the defender already in orbit.

Thus, economics based space deterrence strategies based on the threat of denial or punishment via attacks on CLOCs that are focused on limited means, ways, and ends do not require threats of vital interior, population, or civilizational damage. Space deterrence does not need to rely on uncontrollable escalation to be effective.

Space-power, like seapower, is dynamic and not suited to theories of nuclear deterrence that relies on ever-alert but static forces, including nuclear forces, on threats of uncontrollable escalation, or are prone to believing actual space warfare is “unthinkable.” Rather,
space warfare is a type of limited warfare

that, if limited to the space domain, is likely to be relatively bloodless, especially compared to land warfare. Space warfare is also extremely dynamic, just like the space domain itself, where rapid change and innovation will check any attempt to keep the domain static and unchanging. Space warfare, especially its most limited forms such as jamming and minor physical attacks on solitary satellites or systems, will also probably occur increasingly often. Therefore,
